description: Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic
summary:
Martian Map tells an astronaut where it is safe to walk on Mars, and for how long, before they step outside.

We built a 3D map of three real sites (Gale crater, Jezero delta, Nili Planum) from NASA data: HiRISE terrain, CRISM minerals, THEMIS thermal inertia, weather, and radiation measured by Curiosity. On this map our planner builds three routes to the points you choose: least radiation, least oxygen, most science. Each route is costed with real walking physics and checked by a simulator of the crew member’s fatigue, heat and oxygen.

The planner also forecasts dust devils and picks a safer start time. If a vortex still crosses the route, our AI path planner finds the shortest safe way around it in about a second, then chooses between waiting and going round.

This matters because Earth is 4 to 24 light-minutes away. On Mars, the crew must be able to decide on the spot.
details:
Project Details

Martian Map helps an astronaut plan a walk on Mars before stepping outside. We built it from real NASA data: HiRISE terrain and photos, CRISM minerals, THEMIS thermal inertia, weather from REMS and MEDA, and radiation measured by Curiosity. For each of our three sites (Gale crater, Jezero delta and Nili Planum) that adds up to about thirty map layers.

You click a base and a few points you want to visit, and the planner gives you three routes: one that hides from radiation, one that saves the most oxygen, and one that gets the most science. For every route you see the time, distance, climb, oxygen, battery, radiation dose and the chance of meeting a dust devil. We cost each step with real walking physics, such as how much energy a step takes and how deep a boot sinks in loose sand. Then a small simulator of the crew member walks the plan: it checks fatigue, heat, water and whether there is enough oxygen to get back. If the person would get stuck somewhere, the planner changes the route.

The part we are proudest of is how it deals with dust devils. Our forecast model estimates when and where they are likely, so the planner picks a start time that avoids most of them. In our tests that cuts the expected encounters by about 40 % at Gale and about half at Jezero. If a vortex still heads for the route during the walk, the traveller stops, and our AI path planner (an A* search over the terrain) finds the shortest safe way around it in about a second. Then the system compares waiting for the vortex to pass with going round, and takes whichever costs less time.

We think this matters because a crew on Mars cannot wait four to twenty-four minutes for an answer from Earth. A tool that already knows the terrain, the weather and the crew’s limits lets them decide on the spot. The same planner can also drive a rover, with its own physics for wheels, motors and solar panels.

We wrote the data processing, physics and planning in Python (numpy, matplotlib) and the 3D map in three.js. Our demo film is rendered straight from the map in the browser.

Along the way we had to be careful about a few things. We chose real data over made-up data. We kept to safety limits for oxygen, battery and radiation. We treated the time of day as part of the plan, because light, temperature and dust devils all change with the hour. And we are open about what is simplified: radiation is spread over the terrain from one measured sol, and the dust devils on screen are drawn larger than real so they can be seen.

Next we want the map to learn from every landing, to forecast weather and replan on its own, and to make decisions on board without calling Houston. These are ideas for the future, not features we have built yet.
